scope.start: 13b: the baraita of the idol found among broken vessels bought from gentiles (mid-exchange on whether money or *meshikhah* acquires from a gentile)
scope.end: 14b: the school of R. Yishmael's source for blemished offspring, which leaves Devarim 17:1 for the *bamat yachid*

sections.title: The Idol in the Scrap: Money, Meshikhah, or Both from a Gentile?
sections.gist: Continuing the question of whether money or *meshikhah* acquires from a gentile, the Gemara tests a baraita that seems to need both. It reads the baraita four ways: Abaye's mistaken purchase, Rava's appearance of an idol in a Jew's hands, Rav Ashi's money-only reading and Ravina's *meshikhah*-only reading.

bullets.text: The discussion matters for the chapter's theme: a gentile's share in an animal exempts it from the firstborn obligation, so it matters how a gentile's ownership is transferred.

Rashi rules like the reading that money acquires from a gentile. Most Rishonim, Tosafot among them, rule that *meshikhah* does (as Ameimar held), and do not take this sugya's working-through of the money view as decisive.

In practice this governs the sale of *chametz*, the transfer of land for *shemitah*, and selling part of an animal to a gentile to exempt it from the firstborn obligation. Common practice does both, money and *meshikhah*. It also adds a rental of the place where the item stands, since all agree a gentile acquires land with money.
Whether *chalipin* (a symbolic barter, such as with a kerchief) works with a gentile is a further debate among the authorities.

columns: First clause: why he may return it
Latter clause: why he may not

No *mekach ta'ut* claim: once he paid, he should have inspected before pulling

Also a *mekach ta'ut*, but once paid it looks as if a Jew holds an idol, so he casts it away

Money paid, so the idol is his
He neither paid nor pulled; "returns" means reneging on his word
He pulled, so the idol is his

children.title: The Baraita: Pulled Before or After Paying, and a Jewish-Law Stipulation
children.gist: A baraita about an idol found among broken vessels bought from gentiles seems to need both money and *meshikhah*. The Gemara first explains it as a gentile who accepted Jewish law, so that pulling decides.

bullets.text: The Gemara brings an objection to the view that money acquires from a gentile. Baraita: one who buys broken gold or silver vessels from gentiles finds an idol among them. If he pulled it before paying, he may return it. If he pulled after paying, he may not return it, and must cast it into the Dead Sea.
Once the idol is his, he may not profit from it, so it must be destroyed rather than returned for his money.
If money acquires, why mention pulling? Answer: the gentile had accepted that the transaction be judged by Jewish law.
Then why mention money, since pulling alone should suffice? Answer: the baraita means that even though he paid, it depends on pulling. If he pulled, he acquired; if not, he didn't.
The difficulty is that the baraita seems to require both payment and *meshikhah*, which fits neither simple view.

children.title: First Clause: Why May He Return What He Pulled?
children.gist: In the first clause the buyer pulled without paying and may still return the idol. Abaye calls it a *mekach ta'ut*, Rava places the difference in how it looks, and Abaye defends his line.

children.title: Abaye: A Mekach Ta'ut, and Rava's Objection
children.gist: Abaye explains the return as a mistaken purchase; Rava objects that the latter clause is just as mistaken.

bullets.text: The difficulty: in the first clause he pulled before paying and may still return the idol, so pulling alone seems not to acquire.
Abaye: the first clause is a *mekach ta'ut*, since the buyer never wanted to buy the idol.
Rava objects: then the latter clause is a *mekach ta'ut* too, since he doesn't want the idol in either case.

children.title: Rava: Both Mistaken; Payment Makes It Look Like a Jew's Idol
children.gist: For Rava both clauses are mistaken purchases. What differs is whether it appears that an idol is in a Jew's possession.

bullets.text: Rava: both clauses are a *mekach ta'ut*. Where he hasn't paid the dinars, it doesn't look as if an idol is in a Jew's possession, so he may return it.
Where he has paid, it looks as if an idol is in a Jew's possession, so he must cast it away rather than return it.
For Rava, *meshikhah* acquires in both clauses. Money only decides how returning the idol looks: handing back a paid-for idol for a refund would look like selling an idol.
A bystander could see the return in the first clause too. But with no payment, onlookers understand the deal was never completed. The Sages set a general rule aimed at the likeliest misreading.

children.title: Abaye's Reply: Having Paid, He Should Have Inspected
children.gist: Abaye can keep his distinction: a buyer who has already paid is expected to inspect before pulling, so only the first clause is a mistaken purchase.

bullets.text: Abaye could answer: in the first clause he hadn't paid and so hadn't yet inspected, and the sale is mistaken.
In the latter clause, once he paid he should have inspected before pulling. Since he didn't, the sale stands.

Tosafot: ordinarily, payment doesn't create a duty to inspect. Buying from a gentile is different, because the buyer should have considered that an idol might be among the goods. His claim of surprise is already weak, and payment tips it.
If the risk were common and well known, there would be no *mekach ta'ut* claim at all, paid or not.

children.title: Rav Ashi vs. Ravina: One Mode of Acquisition in Both Clauses
children.gist: Two more readings make the clauses consistent. For Rav Ashi only money acquires (gentile law). For Ravina only *meshikhah* does (Jewish law), and "returns" means reneging on a verbal commitment.

children.title: Rav Ashi: Money Acquires; 'Pulled' Is Repeated Wording
children.gist: Under gentile law only money acquires. The latter clause mentions pulling only because the first clause did.

bullets.text: Rav Ashi: the baraita is a transaction under gentile law, where only money acquires. As for the difficulty raised against R. Oshaya's view (why mention pulling?), pulling is not in fact needed.
Pulling doesn't acquire in the first clause, and so it doesn't in the latter clause either. The first clause said "pulled" to show that it is ineffective, so the latter clause repeated the word.
This is the simplest reading of the baraita, and it fits the view that money acquires between a Jew and a gentile.

children.title: Ravina: Meshikhah Acquires; 'Returns' Means Reneging on His Word
children.gist: Under Jewish law pulling acquires in both clauses. The first clause is a buyer who did neither, and who may back out because *mechusar amanah* doesn't apply between a Jew and a gentile.

bullets.text: Ravina: the transaction is under Jewish law. Since pulling acquires in the latter clause, it does in the first clause too.
The first clause means he neither paid nor pulled. "He returns" means he reneges on his verbal commitment and need not complete the purchase.
The tanna had to say so because he holds that reneging on a verbal commitment is *mechusar amanah* (bad faith). That applies between Jews, who are assumed to keep their word.
It doesn't apply when a Jew buys from gentiles: they are not assumed to keep their word, so neither side relies on the other's commitment.
This assessment reflects the fraught relationship between Jewish communities and the surrounding authorities of that era. It is not a timeless claim about interpersonal ethics.

sections.title: Mishnah: Blemished Before or After Consecration: Kedushat Damim or Kedushat Ha'guf
sections.gist: If the permanent blemish came first, only the animal's value is consecrated, and redemption frees it completely. If it was consecrated first, it keeps its restrictions even after redemption. Firstborn and animal tithe follow the stricter rule.

children.title: First Case: Blemished First, Fully Freed by Redemption
children.gist: A permanent blemish before consecration means only the value is consecrated. Once redeemed, the animal is entirely non-sacred, except that a firstborn or tithe animal is sanctified in its body even so.

bullets.text: Animals with a permanent blemish before consecration take only *kedushat damim*. Once redeemed, their offspring can be a firstborn, and the priestly gifts (foreleg, jaw and maw) are owed.
After redemption they become fully non-sacred: shearing and labor are permitted, and their offspring and milk are permitted.

One who slaughters them outside the courtyard is exempt from *karet*, and *temurah* doesn't take effect with them. If they die before redemption, they are redeemed and fed to dogs, and need no burial.
Except the firstborn and the animal tithe: even if blemished before they became sacred, they take *kedushat ha'guf*, like offerings that became blemished after consecration.
This *kedushat damim* is for the altar: the proceeds must buy an offering. That sets it apart from a plain consecration for Temple maintenance.
Firstborn and tithe differ because their sanctity comes from a fact, birth or being counted tenth, not from a declaration. The Torah says the tenth is holy whether "good or bad".

children.title: Second Case: Consecrated First, Restricted Even After Redemption
children.gist: An animal consecrated before its permanent blemish held *kedushat ha'guf*, so even after redemption it stays exempt from firstborn and gifts, barred from shearing and labor, and its offspring and milk are forbidden.

bullets.text: Animals consecrated before their permanent blemish, or with only a temporary blemish at consecration: after redemption their offspring is not a firstborn and no priestly gifts are owed. They are not freed for shearing and labor.
Their offspring conceived before redemption, and their milk, are forbidden after redemption.
One who slaughters them outside the courtyard is liable to *karet*, and *temurah* takes effect with them. If they die before redemption, they may not be redeemed and fed to dogs; they must be buried.
The shearing and labor ban comes from "*tizbach ve'lo gizah, ve'akhalta ve'lo avodah*": slaughter and eat, but don't shear or work. The Sages read it as referring to redeemed, blemished offerings.
Liability for slaughter outside applies where the blemish is one, such as a cataract, that would not be removed from the altar once brought up. *Temurah* works only before redemption.

sections.title: Before Redemption: Kedushat Damim Exempts from Firstborn and Bars Shearing
sections.gist: Two inferences from "once they were redeemed": until then the animal is exempt from firstborn and gifts, and it may not be shorn or worked. The second either supports R. Eliezer or reflects a narrower decree.

children.title: Firstborn and Priestly Gifts: Kedushat Damim Suffices to Exempt
children.gist: Since the obligation starts only at redemption, the tanna holds that even *kedushat damim* exempts from firstborn and gifts.

bullets.text: The obligations of firstborn and gifts apply because the animals were redeemed. Before redemption they are exempt.
So the tanna holds that *kedushat damim* exempts from the firstborn obligation and from the priestly gifts.
The exemption doesn't depend on *kedushat ha'guf*; any sanctity still in place suffices.
Compare a donkey consecrated to Temple maintenance: its foal is exempt from *peter chamor*, though its sanctity has nothing to do with the altar.

children.title: Shearing Before Redemption: Proof for R. Eliezer, or a Decree for Altar Animals?
children.gist: The shearing ban seems to support R. Eliezer's view on Temple maintenance animals. The Sages answer that it may be a decree limited to altar animals, which can be confused with real offerings.

bullets.text: Redemption frees them for shearing and labor, so before redemption shearing and labor are forbidden.
This seems to support R. Eliezer: animals consecrated for Temple maintenance are forbidden for shearing and labor, and *kedushat damim* is like Temple maintenance sanctity.

The Sages reject the proof. An altar animal with *kedushat damim* can be mistaken for an altar animal with *kedushat ha'guf*, so the Sages decreed against shearing and labor, lest one come to violate a Torah prohibition. For Temple maintenance animals no such decree was issued.
Why forbid shearing at all? The ban comes from the verse about offerings, and this animal isn't one; the Temple could even profit from its wool.

The owner tried to make it an offering, and its proceeds must buy one. *Kedushat damim* for the altar is a middle ground, far likelier to be confused with an offering than a plain Temple maintenance gift.

illustration.caption: The Sages' reply to the proof for R. Eliezer (14a): an altar animal with *kedushat damim* looks like a real offering, so shearing and labor were forbidden by decree; no such decree was issued for Temple maintenance animals.

sections.title: Offspring and Milk: When Conceived, When Born, Redeemed Without a Blemish?
sections.gist: Three steps: the Mishnah's case is an offspring conceived before redemption and born after; one born before is redeemed without needing a blemish; and by contrast an unblemished male consecrated for its value takes *kedushat ha'guf* (Rava).

children.title: Conceived Before Redemption, Born After
children.gist: Offspring conceived and born after redemption are obviously permitted, so the Mishnah means conceived before and born after. By inference, one born before redemption is forbidden until redeemed.

bullets.text: If the mother conceived and gave birth after redemption, the offspring is obviously permitted, since it was non-sacred from conception.
So the Mishnah means conceived before redemption and born after: the offspring is permitted though conceived while its mother was consecrated.
Inference: if born before the redemption, the offspring is forbidden until it is redeemed.
Redeeming the mother removes the sanctity from the fetus along with her.

children.title: Redeeming the Offspring of Kedushat Damim: No Blemish Needed
children.gist: Offspring of a *kedushat ha'guf* animal need a blemish before redemption. A baraita rules that offspring of an animal with *kedushat damim* need none, since the subsidiary is not stricter than the primary.

bullets.text: The offspring of an animal with *kedushat ha'guf* is born sanctified and can't be redeemed until it develops a blemish. The Gemara asks about the offspring of an animal with *kedushat damim*: may it be redeemed unblemished?
Baraita: one who consecrates permanently blemished animals for the altar, and they gave birth: the offspring are sold without needing a blemish.
The reason: sanctity does not take effect on them, and the subsidiary should not be stricter than the primary. The mother can be redeemed at once, so the offspring can too.

children.title: Unblemished Male Consecrated for Its Value: Rava's Kedushat Ha'guf
children.gist: The offspring escape altar sanctity only because theirs derives from a blemished mother. Without such a limit, an unblemished male consecrated for its value takes *kedushat ha'guf*, as Rava says.

bullets.text: The baraita's reason implies that the offspring lack altar sanctity only because theirs derives from the mother. Where there is no such derived sanctity, as when one consecrates an unblemished male for its value, it takes *kedushat ha'guf*.
This supports Rava: one who consecrates a male animal for its value, it is sanctified with *kedushat ha'guf*.
The animal is fit for the altar and nothing limits its sanctity, so it becomes an offering itself rather than being sold to buy one.
Rashi limits the rule to value consecrated for the altar, where the aim is to buy an offering. A consecration purely for Temple maintenance would not become *kedushat ha'guf*.

sections.title: Slaughter Outside: R. Elazar Reads 'Liable,' on a Bamat Yachid
sections.gist: R. Elazar reads the Mishnah as imposing liability for offering a blemished animal on a *bamat yachid*, based on Devarim 17:1. The Gemara tests the verse against four other possible uses: firstborn, animal tithe, *temurah* and offspring.

children.title: R. Elazar: Devarim 17:1 Speaks of the Bamat Yachid
children.gist: Where the Mishnah says "exempt," R. Elazar teaches "liable": lashes for offering a blemished animal on a *bamat yachid*, since the public altar is covered by a different verse.

bullets.text: The Mishnah says one who slaughters them outside is exempt. R. Elazar teaches "liable" instead, and refers the Mishnah to a *bamat yachid*, a private altar: not *karet* for slaughter outside, but lashes for offering a blemished animal there.

R. Elazar's source: "You shall not sacrifice to the Lord an ox or a sheep in which is a blemish" (Devarim 17:1). The great public altar is already covered by "Blind or broken… you shall not sacrifice these" (Vayikra 22:22). So the verse applies to a *bamat yachid*, at a time when such altars were permitted.

children.title: Four Other Uses for the Verse: Firstborn, Animal Tithe, Temurah, Offspring
children.gist: Each proposed alternative is a sanctity that takes hold despite a blemish, so one might think it can be offered blemished. Each turns out to have its own source keeping it off the altar.

bullets.text: Across all four cases the same principle emerges: sanctity that takes hold despite a blemish still can't be offered while the animal is blemished. Being holy and being fit to offer are separate questions.

returns_to.note: Builds on the Mishnah's exception: firstborn and animal tithe are sanctified even when blemished first.

chart.caption: Why each case might have needed Devarim 17:1, and where it is already taught
columns: Why one might think it may be offered blemished
Where its exclusion is already taught
rows: Sanctified even with a permanent blemish
Explicit: "lameness or blindness… you shall not sacrifice it" (Devarim 15:19–21)
Sacred even blemished: "he shall not inquire whether it be good or bad" (Vayikra 27:33)
"It and its substitute shall be holy": compared to the original
Sacred even blemished, on account of the mother
School of R. Yishmael: "your sacred items… and your vows" (Devarim 12:26)

children.title: Firstborn: Its Own Explicit Verse
children.gist: A firstborn is sanctified even when blemished, but Devarim 15 already says a blemished firstborn is not offered.

bullets.text: Objection: apply the verse to a firstborn. Since it is sanctified even when permanently blemished, one might think it may also be offered blemished.
Answer: for the firstborn it is explicit: "if there be any blemish therein, lameness or blindness… you shall not sacrifice it" (Devarim 15:19–21).

children.title: Animal Tithe: A Gezerah Shavah from the Firstborn
children.gist: The tithe is holy "good or bad," but "passing" links it to the firstborn, which is not offered blemished.

bullets.text: Objection: apply it to the animal tithe, which is sacred even when blemished: "he shall not inquire whether it be good or bad" (Vayikra 27:33).

Answer: a *gezerah shavah* links "passing" said of the tithe (Vayikra 27:32) with "passing" said of the firstborn (Shemot 13:12). As a blemished firstborn isn't offered, neither is a blemished tithe animal.

children.title: Temurah: Compared to the Original
children.gist: A *temurah* becomes sacred even when blemished, but "it and its substitute" puts it on a par with the original offering.

bullets.text: Objection: apply it to a *temurah*, which becomes sacred even when blemished: "a good for a bad, or a bad for a good… both it and that for which it is substituted shall be holy" (Vayikra 27:10).
Answer: "it and that for which it is substituted" compares the *temurah* to the original. As the original isn't offered blemished, neither is the *temurah*.

children.title: Offspring: R. Zeira's Objection, Rava's Answer from the School of R. Yishmael
children.gist: R. Zeira proposes blemished offspring of offerings. Rava answers from Devarim 12:26, which equates them with vowed offerings, so Devarim 17:1 is left for the *bamat yachid*.

bullets.text: R. Zeira objects: apply the verse to offspring of offerings. They are sacred even when blemished, on account of their mother, so one might think they may be offered blemished.

Rava: the school of R. Yishmael derived it from "Only your sacred items which you have, and your vows" (Devarim 12:26). "Your sacred items" are *temurot*, "which you have" are offspring, and "your vows" likens them to a vowed offering, which is not offered blemished.
So Devarim 17:1 must refer to the *bamat yachid*, as R. Elazar says.

sections.continues: The Gemara continues through the Mishnah's clauses on 14b: why an animal blemished before consecration doesn't make a *temurah* sacred, and why it may be redeemed after death (Rav: this is R. Shimon's view).

key_terms.sense: acquisition by pulling a movable object
key_terms.definition: A formal act of acquisition in which the buyer pulls or draws a movable object into his possession. Under rabbinic law it, rather than payment, completes a sale of movables between Jews.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara asks whether *meshikhah* or money acquires between a Jew and a gentile, reading a baraita about an idol found among broken vessels four ways.

key_terms.definition: A transaction made under a basic mistake about what was sold, which the aggrieved party may cancel.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Abaye explains why the buyer may return the idol as a *mekach ta'ut*; Rava holds that both clauses are mistaken purchases, and Abaye replies that a buyer who has paid is expected to inspect.

key_terms.sense: bad faith in reneging on a verbal commitment
key_terms.definition: The moral fault of backing out of a verbal agreement that has no binding act of acquisition behind it. It is legally allowed but considered a breach of faith.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Ravina reads "he returns" as reneging on a verbal commitment, which the tanna counts as bad faith between Jews but not toward a gentile.

key_terms.sense: sanctity of an animal's monetary value
key_terms.definition: A consecration that attaches to an animal's value rather than to its body. The animal itself is not offered; it is redeemed or sold and the money goes to its sacred purpose.
key_terms.on_this_daf: An animal blemished before consecration takes only *kedushat damim*. Before redemption this still exempts it from the firstborn obligation and bars shearing, and its offspring may be redeemed without a blemish.

key_terms.sense: inherent sanctity of the animal's body
key_terms.definition: A consecration that attaches to the animal itself, making it an offering for the altar. It is not removed by redemption alone, which requires a blemish and leaves residual restrictions.
key_terms.on_this_daf: An animal consecrated before its blemish, and a firstborn or tithe animal even if blemished first, has *kedushat ha'guf*. Rava holds that an unblemished male consecrated for its value takes it too.

key_terms.sense: substituting one animal for a consecrated one
key_terms.definition: Declaring an unconsecrated animal a substitute for a consecrated one. It is forbidden, yet the substitute becomes sacred along with the original.
key_terms.on_this_daf: *Temurah* does not take effect with an animal blemished before consecration, but does with one consecrated first. A blemished *temurah* can't be offered, because the verse compares it to the original.

key_terms.definition: An altar built by an individual for his own offerings, permitted in the periods before the Temple when private altars were allowed.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Elazar reads the Mishnah as imposing lashes for offering a blemished animal on a *bamat yachid*, based on Devarim 17:1, and the Gemara defends that reading of the verse.

judgment_calls: The four readings of the baraita are grouped in two: the first-clause debate between Abaye and Rava (s3) and the two consistency readings of Rav Ashi and Ravina (s7). A flat list of four sibling readings was also reasonable. The grouping follows the text, where Abaye's reply (13b.11) belongs to the Abaye–Rava exchange.

The shiur's halakhic summary (Rashi vs. most Rishonim, chametz/shemitah/firstborn practice) has no corresponding Gemara line, so it is placed as shiur bullets on the parent section s1 rather than as a separate section.
The Mishnah is split into its two cases (s11, s12). The firstborn and tithe exception stays in the first case, where it falls in the text, rather than getting its own child.
14a.5 and 14a.6–7 are grouped as the two 'before redemption' inferences (s13). The alternative was a separate top-level section for each Mishnah clause the Gemara analyzes.

Rava's ruling on an unblemished male consecrated for its value (14b.3) is kept under the offspring discussion, because the Gemara derives it by contrast with the baraita's reasoning. It could stand as its own top-level section.
The four challenges to R. Elazar's verse are nested as children of s22 under s20, with a chart. Flattening them into bullets of s20 was also possible, but each has its own challenge and source.
s22 carries a returns_to link to the Mishnah's firstborn/tithe exception (s11). That is a thematic link rather than an explicit return, and it could be omitted.
coverage_notes: Lines 13b.7–13b.14 are covered at the start of this shiur (the previous essay tail ended with Ameimar and ona'ah); the essay material is used there, so no section is flagged Gemara text only.
The essay calls the scrap-metal source a mishnah in Avodah Zarah; the text calls it a baraita. Followed the text.

The essay's account of 13b.8 is garbled: it says 'even the beginning involves meshicha… the transaction takes effect but the buyer may still withdraw.' The text: the gentile accepted Jewish law; even though money was paid, acquisition depends on pulling; then the first clause is difficult (13b.9). Followed the text.
The essay attributes the view that Temple maintenance animals are forbidden in shearing and labor to 'Rabbi Elazar'; the text (14a.6) has R. Eliezer. Followed the text.

The essay attributes the private-altar reading to 'Rabbi Eliezer' and frames it as a dissent from the Mishnah's majority. The text (14b.4–5) has R. Elazar, who teaches the Mishnah itself as 'liable' and refers it to a private altar. Followed the text.
The essay says 'Rav Zevid' raises the offspring case and 'the Gemara responds.' The text: R. Zeira objects and Rava answers from the school of R. Yishmael. Followed the text.

The essay's halakhic summary is internally inconsistent about which mode most Rishonim adopt and why (it also says the sugya acknowledged Abaye as a minority view). The outline gives only the consistent core: Rashi follows money, most Rishonim including Tosafot follow meshikhah (as Ameimar held, in line with the previous shiur), and practice does both.
The donkey/peter chamor example, Tosafot on inspection, and Rashi's limit on Rava are the lecturer's material and are marked as shiur.

The essay's Mishnah overview discusses the temurah and died-before-redemption rulings in detail; the Gemara's treatment of those clauses (14b.14–14b.19 and into 15a) falls outside this outline's scope.
The essay's remark that this Mishnah also appears in Chullin and is treated at length in Temurah is not included.
